points.description: Correctly identifies/sets up the key structure: the lines AT_A, BT_B, CT_C are concurrent at a point P (e.g. via the known property that AT_A is the isogonal/related line through the tangency of the mixtixilinear incircle, or by Ceva/trig/inversion arguments). Must be proved, not just asserted.

levels.says: States concurrency of AT_A, BT_B, CT_C (or a key lemma such as T_A, I, and the arc midpoint of BAC being collinear) without a valid proof.
Proves the lemma or concurrency with only minor gaps.

points.description: Uses the concurrency point P to show P has equal power with respect to the three circles (ADT_A), (BET_B), (CFT_C), e.g. by showing PA·PT_A = PB·PT_B = PC·PT_C or via radical axis/inversion computation. The circles meet line AT_A again at T_A, so the power of P is determined by PA·PT_A.

Shows a second point with equal power (e.g. the incenter I, or the point where the radical axes meet, or the radical center/line argument) so the three circles share a radical axis (are coaxial), and that this gives two common points X and Y (the circles intersect in two points, e.g. since a point such as D, E, or F lies inside/on the circle configuration or a common point on the axis has negative power).

levels.says: Gets coaxiality/common radical axis but does not justify that the circles actually meet in two points.

rubric.notes: Full marks need a proof of concurrency of AT_A, BT_B, CT_C, then a power-of-a-point/radical axis argument giving a common axis and two common intersection points. Partial credit for proving concurrency alone (about 3/7). Equivalent alternative methods earn full credit; minor computational slips lose little.
